design-concepts-1-elements-of-design-q1: Texture: the chalkboard-look background. Line: the white hand-drawn lines between sections. Shape: the round price badges. (Space, the wide gaps between drinks and food, or colour, white on a dark board, would also earn the mark.)
design-concepts-1-elements-of-design-q2: Line: the white hand-drawn lines divide the menu into sections, so customers can see where the drinks end and the food begins and scan the board quickly. Shape: the round price badges repeat the same shape for every price, so prices are easy to find and look consistent.
design-concepts-2-principles-of-design-q: (a) Dominance (emphasis): the huge orange heading is the first thing the eye goes to. (b) Unity (repetition): the same small logo repeated in each corner ties the flyer together. (c) Unity (proximity): grouping the times in one box shows they belong together.

Emphasis could be created with contrast and proportion: make the date much larger and bold, and use a colour that contrasts with the background, such as dark blue on a light panel. The date then becomes a clear focal point that readers notice straight after the heading, instead of being lost in the small grey text.
design-concepts-3-elements-and-principle: Space creates dominance. The large temperature has a lot of empty space around it, so nothing competes with it and the eye goes there first. This means the viewer can read today's temperature at a glance, which is the most important information on the screen.

Shape creates unity through repetition. The three forecast cards use the same rounded rectangle shape in the same size, set in one row. Repeating the shape makes the forecast read as one group, so the screen looks organised and consistent.
design-concepts-4-typography-q1: 1. Body text size: use at least 14 pt for the body text, because many residents have poor eyesight and need to read it without straining or glasses. 2. Typeface: use a clear sans serif such as Arial for the body text, because its simple letter shapes are easier to recognise at a glance than a decorative typeface.
design-concepts-4-typography-q2: Justified alignment stretches the spaces between words so both edges are straight. This leaves uneven gaps, sometimes forming 'rivers' of white space down the page, which makes the text harder to follow. Residents with poor eyesight would find it even harder to read, so left alignment is better.
design-concepts-5-compositional-rules-q1: The rule of thirds divides the frame into a 3 x 3 grid using two horizontal and two vertical lines. Key items are placed on the lines or where they cross, instead of in the centre, so the composition looks balanced and more interesting.
design-concepts-5-compositional-rules-q2: A grid would give every item a consistent position and equal gaps, so the title, date, photo and ticket link no longer float with random spacing. Alignment would line the items up on one edge, such as the left margin, which connects them visually and makes the post look neat, organised and easy to read in order.
design-concepts-6-analysing-existing-pro: Colour: the event name is in large white text over the dark fireworks photo, so it contrasts strongly with the background and is easy to read.

Shape creates unity. The four buttons (Map, Food, Parking, Tickets) are the same size and shape, repeated in one row, so they read as one set of related choices and the page looks consistent. An improvement would be to give each button a small icon, such as a car for Parking, so visitors can recognise them faster.
design-concepts-7-modifying-and-annotati: 1. Make the Saturday hours larger and bold, and move them above the logo, so they become the focal point and people notice the new hours first. 2. Reduce the five fonts to two, one for the heading and one for the body, so the post looks consistent and professional instead of cluttered.
Opening hours moved to the top and enlarged to 36 pt bold (element: size and space). This creates emphasis, so the new Saturday hours are the first thing the viewer notices.

hardware-1-cpu-and-memory-q2: Laptop A has a 256 GB SSD, while Laptop B has a 1 TB HDD, so B holds about four times more files, which suits a student storing large videos. But A's SSD has no moving parts, so it is faster to open programs and files and is less likely to be damaged if the laptop is knocked in a school bag.

hardware-3-operating-systems-q2: Advantage: Linux is free, so the business saves the licence cost for five laptops. Disadvantage: some business software only runs on Windows, and staff used to Windows may need training, which costs time.

impacts-of-technology-u3-3-social-networ: Fewer people buy printed newspapers because they can read free news on social media, so the paper could no longer cover its printing and delivery costs. Publishing online only is cheaper and reaches readers on their phones.

application-skills-u3-5-software-licence: Proprietary software is owned by a company. It is closed source, so users cannot see or change the code, and it is used under a paid licence with restrictions on how it can be used.

Support: Microsoft provides guaranteed support and regular updates, but LibreOffice relies on community help, which may be harder for a school with limited IT staff. Both can open common documents, but formatting may differ.
application-skills-u3-6-spreadsheet-desi: Mixed prices such as '$2', '2.00' and 'two dollars' are a mix of text and numbers. The spreadsheet cannot calculate or sort text correctly, so totals will be wrong.
